title: Clausewitz and Moltke Solved Our Leadership Problem. We Just Never Learned It.
author: Uwe Mierisch
summary: Uwe Mierisch, writing about his NewPDP product-development model, opens with a story of a boss who told his engineers to weld a prototype together with the newest engine and "not worry about anything else," which rescued a dying product and convinced him that leadership matters. He then separates leadership from management using John Kotter: management copes with complexity, while leadership copes with change by setting direction and aligning people. Drawing on Clausewitz and Moltke, he argues that a company has three levels rather than two, namely purpose, strategy and tactics, and that each needs its own leadership. Purpose is set by the executive board and must stay stable, tactics belong to the people closest to the action under mission command, and strategy is the constant reassessment of the situation after every move. A boss, in his definition, is the person who takes responsibility for what others do, which only works if the boss contributes and stays close to the work. Management is recast as the deployment that reduces execution complexity, and he warns that tracking, monitoring and justifying are not management at all.
points: Leadership and management are different jobs: management copes with complexity through planning and organizing, while leadership copes with change by setting a direction people follow.
Organizations work better with three levels (purpose, strategy, tactics) than with a simple split between doers and managers, and the board owns a purpose that must stay stable over years.

Mission command means telling people what must be achieved and why, then letting the person on the spot decide how, which only works inside a shared rhythm with visible tasks and clear responsibilities.
Strategy is not a roadmap but the continuous reassessment of each move against the purpose, and strategists must be present where the work happens instead of in an ivory tower.
A boss is defined by taking responsibility for what others do, and good management is the up-front deployment that removes avoidable complexity, not tracking, monitoring or justifying.
quotes: Management copes with complexity. It plans, budgets, organizes and controls. It makes sure a large system runs reliably.
Leadership copes with change. It sets a direction, aligns people behind it and gets them moving.
The superior says what needs to be achieved and why. The how is decided by the person on the spot.
If you only know the what, you cannot sensibly deviate when the situation changes. If you know the intent, you can.
Strategy is what happens between purpose and plan: after every move, reassessing where you stand and choosing the next move.
Not just for what they do themselves. Every professional, every engineer, every expert does that. But for what others do.
Only someone who contributes can take responsibility for what others do. The boss has to engage with the issues, know the situation, test the arguments and do their own part.
Leadership says where we are going. Management positions the team so it can get there.
